Then let's go further back, past Andromeda and past every galaxy, to the oldest light there is.

**The static between channels**

About 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe was a hot, glowing fog of plasma, so dense that light couldn't travel far before bumping into a free electron. Then it cooled enough for electrons to settle into atoms, and almost all at once the fog cleared. Light that had been trapped was suddenly free to travel.

That light is still traveling. It has been stretched by 13.8 billion years of cosmic expansion, from a yellowish-white glow into faint microwaves, and it fills every direction of the sky evenly. We call it the cosmic microwave background.

You've probably encountered it. On old analog televisions, tuned between channels, a small fraction of the snowy static, roughly one percent, came from this light. People watched the afterglow of the universe's birth hissing on their screens and changed the channel.

**You are made of the rest of the story**

The hydrogen in your body, in every water molecule, has existed since the first few minutes of the universe. It's essentially as old as time.

Almost everything heavier came later, and from violence. The carbon in your cells and the oxygen you're breathing were forged inside stars that lived and died before the Sun existed. The calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood were scattered across space when stars exploded. Some of the heavier elements, possibly including much of the gold on Earth, may have been made when the collapsed cores of dead stars, neutron stars, spiraled into each other and collided.

Then gravity gathered that debris into a cloud, the cloud into a Sun and planets, and over billions of years some of it organized itself into chemistry that could copy itself, then into cells, then into something that could look up.

So when you see that faint smudge of Andromeda, it isn't quite a stranger sending a message to a stranger. It's one part of the universe's leftover material seeing another part. Carl Sagan put it this way: we are a way for the cosmos to know itself.

**The edge we'll never cross**

One last strange fact. Because space is expanding, and that expansion is accelerating, there are galaxies we can see today whose light, emitted now, will never reach us. The most distant galaxies are slipping past a horizon. In the very far future, perhaps a hundred billion years from now, astronomers in our merged Milky Way and Andromeda galaxy may look out and see only their own home galaxy surrounded by darkness.
